SUTR-013 — SuperUnicode East Asian Spacing (SUEAS)

The binary-mapped East Asian width schema, the compiled East_Asian_Spacing and East_Asian_Width range tables, the zero-allocation O(1) width and column-span engine, the contextual inter-character spacing resolver, and the single-pass cell-grid engine across the Bridge and Supplement blocks and the Native & Neography Plane

Standard ID: SUTR-013
Status: 0.1.0 — Published
Scope: The binary-mapped East Asian width schema, the compiled East_Asian_Spacing and East_Asian_Width range tables, the zero-allocation O(1) width and column-span engine, the contextual inter-character spacing resolver, and the single-pass cell-grid engine across the Bridge and Supplement blocks and the Native & Neography Plane
Applies to: SUCD (SUAS-012), SUAS-014 (SUVTL), SUTR-0 (SUCS Core), SUTR-1 (SUTF), SUTR-6 (Bridge), the SUF vector font engine, terminal emulators, GUI text renderers, and every grid or proportional layout consumer
Last updated: 2026-10-22
Source: docs/sutr/SUTR-013-sueas.md — this page is generated from it, and the repository copy governs where they differ.

1. Overview

Where UTR #59 East Asian Spacing describes — as an informative draft — the algorithm and the data by which a small amount of visible space is inserted between East Asian scripts and other scripts to improve readability, SUTR-013 (SUEAS) establishes the equivalent contract for SuperUnicode: the binary-mapped width metrics, the contextual spacing rules, and the zero-allocation layout engines required to resolve East Asian character widths (Fullwidth, Halfwidth, Ambiguous, and Neutral) and proportional inter-character spacing across 31-bit SuperUnicode text streams in O(1) constant time.

The report answers four questions that a renderer must share:

  1. What is the grid width of a codepoint — one column or two — and what width category (Fullwidth, Halfwidth, Narrow, Wide, Ambiguous) does it carry?
  2. Does a visible auto-space belong between two adjacent clusters?
  3. How wide is a whole stream in terminal cells, and how many auto-spaces would it receive?
  4. How do all of the above stay reachable in O(1) per glyph, with no heap and no runtime property-file parse?

1.1 Relation to UTR #59

SUEAS is the SuperUnicode analog of UTR #59. It adopts that report's framing: the spacing classification and the width classification are derived properties of the Unicode Character Database, maintained separately from the basic code-chart information, and the algorithm that inserts the visible space is documented on its own schedule rather than on the Unicode release cycle. Where this report and UTR #59 differ, this report governs for SuperUnicode.

The decisive difference is the execution model. UTR #59 is an informative document: it describes a runtime East_Asian_Spacing property query, a dynamic East_Asian_Width (EAW) parse, and a heuristic grid-alignment algorithm that adds the visible space in a post-pass. SUEAS is an engine specification. Both properties are compiled at build time into immutable, byte-aligned, static range tables; a codepoint resolves its spacing value, its width value, and its column span with a bounded binary search — no property-file parse, no libc, no heap. The kernel never reads a data file at run time.

1.2 Scope

This report specifies the address-space zones and their renderability (§2), the compiled binary range schema and its descriptor geometry (§3), the contextual spacing-resolution contract (§4), the zero-allocation grid and space-count engines (§5), the algorithmic default for unlisted characters (§6), the normative requirements (§7), and the reference implementation and its data curation (§8). It does not define a glyph rasterizer, a font format, or a line-breaking algorithm; those remain with the SUF vector font engine and SUVTL. It also does not define the East Asian contents: the compiled range tables are version data, curated from the Unicode 18.0.0 UCD and the UTR #59 derived data file, and may be revised independently of the engine that reads them.

1.3 Key architectural concepts

1.3.1 Pre-compiled binary width classifications

SUEAS replaces runtime EAW property parsing with static, byte-packed width descriptors (sueas_width_entry_t). Each 31-bit SuperUnicode codepoint maps directly to an explicit width category (Fullwidth, Halfwidth, Narrow, Wide, or Ambiguous) and proportional-scaling flags, resolved from two merged, sorted, non-overlapping range tables — one for East_Asian_Spacing, one for East_Asian_Width.

1.3.2 Zero-allocation grid and spacing resolution in O(1)

During text rendering and terminal cell-grid allocation, the microkernel evaluates character widths and conditional spacing adjustments — including punctuation adjustment and CJK-to-Latin spacing — via direct memory indexing in constant time per glyph, with a fixed 12-byte previous-cluster record on the frame and not a single heap allocation (malloc/free).

1.3.3 Modular technical report compliance

Because specialized East Asian grid formatting and proportional spacing adjustments are modular display features rather than core microkernel bootstrapping requirements, SUEAS is categorized as a modular SUTR technical specification: a headless server kernel may omit it entirely without impacting core system integrity (§1.6).

1.3.4 Neography and conscript spacing integration

Because SUEAS decouples width calculations from the legacy Unicode blocks, a user-space toolchain can extend its binary lookup tables to define custom grid widths, fixed-pitch metrics, and proportional spacing rules for logographic and mixed-script conlangs within the Native & Neography Plane (0x160000–0x16FFFF) using the exact same structural rules.

1.4 Spacing specification matrix

Concern UTR #59 SUEAS
Spacing classification Runtime derived-property query Compiled O(log R) range table
Width classification Dynamic EAW parse Compiled O(log R) range table
Column span Heuristic, per consumer column_units in the binary descriptor
Spacing adoption Post-pass grid alignment Single-pass boundary rule (§4.3)
Stream measurement Per-glyph, with allocation One pass, zero allocation
Memory Not specified Zero allocation, caller-owned descriptors
Repertoire split One data file, all scripts Two merged range tables, tagged by zone

1.5 Cross-references

  • SUAS-012 (SUCD) — the offline reference layer: the human-readable East_Asian_Spacing and East_Asian_Width manifests from which SUEAS's binary tables are compiled.
  • SUAS-014 (SUVTL) — vertical text layout: SUEAS supplies the per-character column spans that SUVTL's line and column passes consume.
  • SUTR-10 (SUCM) — the conformance model: SUEAS is a REFERENCE-kind report that nevertheless ships a reference unit (sutr_sueas), and holds the zero-allocation and O(1) mandate for every query on its hot path.

1.6 Omitting SUEAS

Because core operating system primitives, file paths, and kernel IPC channels require strict text safety rather than East Asian grid display, SUEAS is categorized as a modular technical report: a lightweight server kernel or a headless environment may omit it entirely without impacting core system integrity. The engine, the record layout, and the resolution contract are architectural; the East Asian contents are version data (§8).

2. Background

East Asian established typography defines that a small amount of visible space between East Asian scripts and other scripts improves readability. This visible space is not a typographic space character; it is a rendering adjustment applied at the boundary between two adjacent clusters. SUEAS preserves the structure of that idea while replacing its delivery mechanism.

There are two derived properties involved:

  • East_Asian_Spacing (EAS) — the classification that drives the spacing algorithm, with the values O (Other), N (Narrow), W (Wide), and C (Conditional). The value W marks an East Asian script character that receives visible space against a Narrow neighbour; N marks a non-East-Asian character that receives visible space against a Wide neighbour; C marks a character whose treatment depends on the language context (a punctuation such as the full stop or the comma).
  • East_Asian_Width (EAW) — the UAX #11 width classification, with the values N (Neutral), A (Ambiguous), H (Halfwidth), W (Wide), F (Fullwidth), and Na (Narrow).

A traditional implementation resolves both at run time: it parses a properties file or builds an in-memory index, queries East_Asian_Spacing for each character, dereferences the EAW value for each character, and then applies a grid-alignment heuristic in a post-pass over the laid-out line. Every one of those steps may allocate, and none of them is bounded by the microkernel's O(1) guarantee.

There are several reasons to prefer the compiled form:

First, the two properties change only with a Unicode release (or with a UTR #59 data revision), so a runtime parse re-derives a constant on every boot. SUEAS compiles the constant once.

Second, the merged range form is exact and self-verifying: the ranges are strictly ascending, non-overlapping, and gap-separated, so a bounded binary search is a total function, and the invariant is checked by the unit test rather than merely asserted.

Third, a renderer's hot path asks a small number of questions — the column span, the category, the two spacing values, and the boundary decision. SUEAS answers all of them from the same two tables, so a terminal row, a wrapped paragraph, and a proportional-spacing pass share one source of truth.

Finally, separating the spacing and width contents from the engine that reads them makes the data maintainable with normal editorial tools. In SUEAS the editorial artifact is the SUCD manifest, a line-oriented text file — not a runtime parse.

2.1 Address-space zones

SUEAS operates over the 31-bit SUCS codepoint space and recognizes the same address-space zones as the rest of the standard. A width query is admissible only against a renderable zone.

Zone Range Renderable
Bridge 0x00000000–0x0010FFFF Yes
SCP 0x00110000–0x0011FFFF No
RNUR 0x00160000–0x0016FFFF Yes
Native rest of 0x00120000–0x7FFFFFEF Yes
Trap 0x7FFFFFF0–0x7FFFFFFE No
Sentinel 0x7FFFFFFF No
ExtSUCS > 0x7FFFFFFF No

The East Asian repertoire spans the Bridge Plane:

Block Range Role
CJK Symbols and Punctuation, Kana, Hangul 0x3000–0x33FF, 0x3040–0x30FF, 0xAC00–0xD7A3, … Wide script characters
Halfwidth and Fullwidth Forms 0xFF00–0xFFEF Fullwidth and Halfwidth forms
CJK Unified Ideographs 0x4E00–0x9FFF Wide ideographs
RNUR carve-out 0x00160000–0x0016FFFF Conscript and logographic conlangs

2.2 The RNUR neography carve-out

A toolchain may adapt the SUEAS engine to a logographic or mixed-script conlang within the Native & Neography Plane. The neography set of a codepoint is (codepoint − 0x00160000) >> 8, so an RNUR codepoint maps to a set index in 0x00–0xFF. A renderer that defines custom grid widths or fixed-pitch metrics for such a script tags its records with the Native plane flag and grid-snap flag; the resolver treats them exactly as it treats Bridge characters.

3. The compiled East Asian width schema

3.1 The binary range record

Both compiled tables are arrays of fixed-size, byte-aligned, padding-free records of 12 bytes, so a consumer may map an array of them directly from a compiled image with no decode step.

Field Type Offset Size Meaning
first uint32_t 0 4 First codepoint of the range
last uint32_t 4 4 Last codepoint of the range
value uint32_t 8 4 The sueas_spacing_t or sueas_eaw_t value

The exact field order is a compile-time invariant, proven with offsetof-based negative-array-bound assertions, so the layout cannot drift.

3.2 The width descriptor

The per-codepoint result of a query is the fixed-size sueas_width_entry_t of 8 bytes, padding-free.

Field Type Offset Size Meaning
codepoint uint32_t 0 4 The raw 31-bit SuperUnicode codepoint
spacing_flags uint16_t 4 2 Packed spacing and adjustment flags (§3.3)
width_category uint8_t 6 1 The sueas_width_category_t (§3.2.1)
column_units uint8_t 7 1 Grid column span: 1 ordinary, 2 wide

3.2.1 The width category

The width category named by the seeding sketch is a projection of the two compiled properties:

Category Value Projected from
SUEAS_WIDTH_NEUTRAL 0 Neither East Asian nor an ordinary starter
SUEAS_WIDTH_NAR 1 East_Asian_Spacing = N (one column, ordinary)
SUEAS_WIDTH_WID 2 East_Asian_Spacing = W (two columns, East Asian)
SUEAS_WIDTH_FULL 3 East_Asian_Width = F
SUEAS_WIDTH_HALF 4 East_Asian_Width = H
SUEAS_WIDTH_AMB 5 East_Asian_Width = A, not Wide spacing

The East_Asian_Spacing value wins for a Wide or Narrow character, because that is the value the spacing algorithm acts on.

3.3 Spacing and adjustment flags

Flag Bit Meaning
SUEAS_FLAG_PROPORTIONAL 0 Allow proportional micro-spacing
SUEAS_FLAG_GRID_SNAP 1 Force alignment to the character grid
SUEAS_FLAG_PUNCT_ADJUST 2 Apply halfwidth punctuation centering
SUEAS_FLAG_WIDE 3 Has a Wide East_Asian_Spacing
SUEAS_FLAG_NARROW 4 Has a Narrow East_Asian_Spacing
SUEAS_FLAG_CONDITIONAL 5 Has a Conditional spacing value
SUEAS_FLAG_EAST_ASIAN 6 Belongs to an East Asian script
SUEAS_FLAG_NATIVE 7 Lies in the Native / neography plane

All defined flag bits fall within SUEAS_FLAG_ASSIGNED_MASK (0x00FF); the bits are disjoint and the mask is the low byte.

3.4 Grid column span

The column_units of a codepoint is 2 for a Wide, Fullwidth, or Ambiguous glyph, and 1 otherwise. Ambiguous resolves to two columns by default, because the default context is an East Asian grid; a consumer that resolves Ambiguous to one column does so through its own policy before measuring. A codepoint in an inadmissible zone has no column span and reports 0.

3.5 The compiled range tables and the bounded search

Two static tables hold the merged, sorted, non-overlapping, gap-separated ranges:

  • East_Asian_Spacing — O = 0, N = 1, W = 2, C = 3.
  • East_Asian_Width — N = 0, A = 1, H = 2, W = 3, F = 4, Na = 5.

A lookup is a standard upper-bound binary search over the sorted table followed by an endpoint test; a codepoint that precedes the first range, or that falls in a gap between ranges, is answered by the algorithmic default of §6. The search is bounded by the table size, hence O(log R), and the table is enumerated for verification through sutr_sueas_spacing_at / sutr_sueas_eaw_at.

The FNV-1a hash of a codepoint (sutr_sueas_hash_codepoint), used by consumers that build their own caches, folds the four little-endian bytes of the codepoint with the standard 2166136261 offset basis and the 16777619 prime.

4. Contextual spacing resolution

4.1 The resolved spacing value

The compiled East_Asian_Spacing value is a property of the character alone. The resolved value that drives the boundary rule depends on two context bits:

  1. Language context. A Conditional (C) value resolves to Narrow when the language context is Chinese, and to Other otherwise. This is how the full stop and the comma behave: they space against East Asian characters in Chinese text and do not elsewhere.
  2. Vertical upright. A Narrow value displayed upright in vertical layout resolves to Other, because the visible space is a horizontal-typography adjustment.

sutr_sueas_resolve_spacing applies both rules and returns the effective value; Wide and Other are unchanged by either context bit.

4.2 The boundary rule

A visible auto-space is inserted exactly at a Wide/Narrow or Narrow/Wide boundary of the resolved values, and nowhere else:

Left Right Space
Wide Narrow Yes
Narrow Wide Yes
Wide Wide No
Narrow Narrow No
Other any No
any Other No

sutr_sueas_needs_space implements the boundary rule alone; it is a pure function of the two resolved values and costs O(1).

4.3 The per-pair decision

sutr_sueas_spacing_decision composes the two: it resolves both codepoints through §4.1 and then applies §4.2, writing a fixed-size sueas_spacing_decision_t of 8 bytes:

Field Type Offset Meaning
space uint8_t 0 1 when a visible space is inserted
tight uint8_t 1 1 when the pair must not break (no space)
reserved uint16_t 2 Must be zero
reserved2 uint32_t 4 Must be zero

Either codepoint in an inadmissible zone, or a NULL descriptor, reports absence.

5. The zero-allocation grid engine

5.1 Stream measurement

sutr_sueas_measure_columns walks a codepoint stream once and writes the number of grid columns each codepoint occupies into a caller-owned array; the return value is the total column span of the whole stream in terminal cells. The caller may pass a NULL array to compute only the total, and a capacity smaller than the stream to write only the prefix — the running total is always complete, following the snprintf convention. The walk is O(n) with a single size_t accumulator and no allocation.

sutr_sueas_measure_columns_ex is the same walk with the language-context and vertical-upright bits of §4.1 threaded through, so a Conditional that resolves to Narrow takes one column and an upright Narrow takes one column.

5.2 Space counting

sutr_sueas_count_spaces counts the auto-spaces the stream would receive: the number of adjacent cluster pairs at a Wide/Narrow or Narrow/Wide boundary of the resolved values, holding only a fixed 12-byte previous-cluster record on the frame. It is O(n) with no allocation, and a non-renderable control character is skipped without breaking adjacency.

5.3 Integration

A terminal emulator uses §5.1 to size a row; a GUI text renderer uses it to decide wrap points; and a proportional-spacing pass uses §5.2 to know how many visible spaces to distribute. All three share the same two tables and the same resolution rules, so a measured width and a rendered width cannot disagree.

6. The algorithmic default

Only codepoints listed in the compiled tables have an explicit value. Every other renderable codepoint falls to the algorithmic default:

  • East_Asian_Spacing = Other (code 0),
  • East_Asian_Width = Neutral (code 0),
  • width category = Neutral,
  • column_units = 1.

This matches the documented defaults of the source data files: the UTR #59 derived data file gives @missing: 0000..10FFFF; O, and the UCD EastAsianWidth.txt gives N to every unlisted codepoint. The default is total: a query against a renderable-but-unlisted codepoint succeeds and returns the default rather than a lookup failure. A query against an inadmissible zone reports absence.

7. Normative requirements

  1. The engine shall be freestanding C99 and shall not call malloc, free, stdio, or a libc string routine on any query path.
  2. A width query shall be O(log R) in the size R of the compiled tables and shall never return a pointer into a heap.
  3. The width descriptor shall be 8 bytes and the range record 12 bytes, with the exact field order of §3.1 and §3.2.
  4. The compiled range tables shall be strictly ascending, non-overlapping, and gap-separated, so the bounded search of §3.5 is exact.
  5. The resolved spacing value shall be a pure function of the compiled value and the two context bits of §4.1.
  6. The boundary rule of §4.2 shall insert a visible space exactly at a Wide/Narrow or Narrow/Wide boundary of the resolved values.
  7. The stream-measurement and space-count engines of §5 shall be O(n) with no allocation.
  8. A query against an inadmissible zone shall report absence rather than a synthesized descriptor.

8. Reference implementation

SUEAS is implemented by include/sutr/sutr_sueas.h and src/sutr/sutr_sueas.c as a freestanding C99 static library (sutr_static), with the host unit tests in tests/test_sutr_sueas.c. It registers with the SuperUnicode Specification Registry & Cross-Reference Engine (SSRE, SUAS-010) as specification SUTR-013 with reference unit sutr_sueas, kind REFERENCE, version 0.1.0, and records the sueas claim in the SuperUnicode Conformance Model (SUCM, SUTR-10) at tier L0.

8.1 The compiled data

The compiled tables are generated from the Unicode Character Database:

Table Source Rows Distribution
East_Asian_Spacing UTR #59 east-asian-spacing.txt 1170 W: 52, N: 736, C: 170, O: 212
East_Asian_Width UCD EastAsianWidth.txt (18.0.0) 1204 N: 883, A: 179, H: 7, W: 125, F: 3, Na: 7

The records are version data: a revision tracks a Unicode release or a UTR #59 data revision, not an engine revision.

8.2 Verification

The unit test suite covers the version and metadata, the compile-time record geometry, zone dispatch and the RNUR carve-out, the FNV-1a hash, the compiled range tables and the algorithmic default, the width query and every failure outcome, the classification predicates, the spacing resolver across the Conditional and vertical rules, the O(n) grid and space-count engines, enumeration and table self-consistency, the taxonomy names, and the SSRE registration.
